description: Somos un equipo de 540, un estudio de desarrollo de software que lleva desde 2014 construyendo soluciones ágiles, sólidas y pragmáticas. Creemos en poner a las personas en el centro de la tecnología y en un software responsable y sostenible: Rev is Dev. Venimos a la NASA Space Apps a aplicar todo eso a los retos del espacio… y a pasarlo en grande.
summary:
**Lunar Landing Site Navigator** helps decide where and when to land at the Moon's south pole. There the Sun barely rises above the horizon, so the local terrain decides whether a lander gets sunlight for its solar panels and keeps Earth in view to communicate. A site that works one week can be in shadow or out of contact the next.

We built an engine that computes the Sun and Earth over the real horizon, using real ephemerides and NASA's LOLA terrain, and checks whether a mission is viable at a given site and date. Mission planners enter a spacecraft's requirements (days on the surface, hours it can survive without Sun, Earth visibility) and get the best sites and dates, each verdict with its reason. If the launch slips, the tool finds a way out. A 3D South Pole Lookout shows the shadows moving, and an onboard landing simulator and a role-playing game bring the same data to the public. Everything is also available through a public REST and GraphQL API.

As Artemis and commercial landers head to the south pole, choosing the landing window decides whether the mission survives.
details:
What it does and how it works

At the lunar south pole the Sun stays a few degrees above the horizon, so ridges and crater rims decide whether a lander gets sunlight and keeps Earth in view. Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers one question: can this mission survive at this site, on these dates?

Our engine computes the positions of the Sun and Earth from real ephemerides and checks them against the actual horizon of each site, built from NASA's LOLA terrain. Sun and Earth are treated as discs, not points. From that it derives visibility windows, the longest night, the longest communication blackout, slope, and Deep Space Network coverage. The planner turns a spacecraft's requirements into a verdict for every day, with the reason, and ranks the best sites and dates. It also shows what happens if the lander touches down off target, and how to recover if the launch slips.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission planners can compare sites and windows in seconds instead of running custom analyses. Students and the public can see why light at the pole is so scarce: a 3D South Pole Lookout where shadows sweep across real terrain, an onboard landing simulator, and an educational role-playing game. All the computations are open through a public REST and GraphQL API, so other teams can build on the same data.

Tools and technologies

  • Engine and API: Node.js and TypeScript, with astronomy-engine for ephemerides, LOLA elevation models (read with geotiff) for horizons, and GraphQL alongside a REST v1 API with an OpenAPI spec. A parity test checks that both APIs always return the same results.
  • Frontend: a static site with no build step, in HTML, CSS and JavaScript modules, three.js for the 3D scenes, and MediaPipe for an optional hand-gesture control. Hosted on GitHub Pages, in English and Spanish.
  • Data: NASA LOLA terrain, NASA Blue Marble imagery, the NASA 3D Z-2 spacesuit model and the Yale Bright Star Catalogue. Results are validated against JPL Horizons and NASA PGDA illumination products, with a public validation matrix.
  • Process: developed with AI assistance (Claude Code), with tests, golden results and code review on every change.

Creativity

The same engine serves very different audiences: a planner's dashboard, a cinematic 3D explorer, a first-person landing with lunar gravity and Apollo-like descent engine figures, and a game where you drive a rover chasing light and Earth before your battery dies.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty first. Every verdict explains its reason, the uncertainty band of the terrain is shown, and the tool warns where results are less reliable, such as near ground level or south of 85°S. We documented the known deviations from NASA's reference products. We also cared about accessibility, performance on modest devices, bilingual content, and keeping everything open and reproducible.
